The newly emerged nestling, still entirely dependent on parental provisioning, weighs approximately 1.2 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.2 grams] at the moment of hatching. This low neonatal mass is characteristic of altricial bird species, where the bulk of growth occurs post-hatching under intensive brooding and feeding by both parents. During the first few days after hatching, the chick undergoes a rapid phase of mass increase as it transitions from yolk-dependent reserves to exogenous feeding, marking the onset of the exotrophic transition.

This timing places the species within the typical range for brood-parasitic finches, where a relatively rapid nestling period reduces exposure to predation. Following fledging, the juveniles are still provisioned by host parents for a period of several weeks before achieving full nutritional independence. The subsequent transition to a free-living juvenile stage is marked by the gradual development of the characteristic elongated tail feathers, which do not fully mature until well into the first year of life.

The age at first successful reproduction, however, is substantially delayed relative to the onset of puberty. Under the same thermal conditions, the first brood is typically produced at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], indicating a prolonged period of sexual maturation and behavioural development at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This extended interval between reaching sexual maturity and actually breeding is common among estrildid finches, where male courtship displays, including the elaborate elongated tail and aerial dances, require a full molt cycle to develop fully before they become effective in attracting mates.

Adult body size in Vidua paradisaea exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, a feature common among brood-parasitic finches where males invest heavily in ornamental plumage for lek-based mating systems.
